title: Temperature Scaling Fits One Parameter. Calibration Is a Function.
summary: A classifier is calibrated when its probability outputs track the frequencies they report. If across the inputs the model assigns probability 0.8, 80% of them really do belong to the positive class, the model is well calibrated at 0.8....
body:
A classifier is calibrated when its probability outputs track the frequencies they report. If across the inputs the model assigns probability 0.8, 80% of them really do belong to the positive class, the model is well calibrated at 0.8. If this holds for every output value, it is well calibrated everywhere. That is the quiet target of nearly every post-hoc calibration method in use — Platt scaling, temperature scaling, isotonic regression — and almost no deployment measures what it actually got. The practice is to fit one of these methods on a held-out set, measure Expected Calibration Error, see it drop, and move on. The problem with this chain is not that the fit is wrong. It is that the quantity we fit, the quantity we measure, and the quantity we claim to control are three different objects whose coincidence requires assumptions almost no classifier satisfies.

## Why this matters now

Three threads converge. First, every frontier LLM is a classifier whose outputs are probabilities, and every post-training step — supervised fine-tuning, RLHF, DPO — has been reported to leave the model badly calibrated at those outputs. Xie, Chen, Lee, and Finn (ICLR/EMNLP 2024) measure the degradation and introduce Adaptive Temperature Scaling to fix it, reporting 10–50% ECE improvements on standard NLG benchmarks. Second, Kumar, Liang, and Ma (NeurIPS 2019) proved that the standard calibrators — Platt and temperature scaling — are *less calibrated than reported*, and that the standard estimators of calibration error cannot tell you by how much. Third, Gupta and Ramdas (ICML 2022) and Popordanoska et al. (NeurIPS 2022) made precise what nobody writing a calibration section quite acknowledges: in a multiclass problem with more than a handful of classes, the strict version of calibration becomes unmeasurable, and we are quietly measuring and fixing a strictly weaker thing. The three results do not conflict. They are three faces of the same identifiability problem.

## What calibration actually is

Fix a classifier $f: \mathcal{X} \to \Delta^{K-1}$ producing a probability vector over $K$ classes, and a label $Y \in \{1, \dots, K\}$. The strongest and only self-consistent notion of calibration is *canonical calibration*: for every probability vector $p \in \Delta^{K-1}$ in the image of $f$,
$$
\Pr(Y = k \mid f(X) = p) = p_k \quad \text{for all } k.
$$
Writing $r_k(p) = \Pr(Y = k \mid f(X) = p)$ for the true conditional, canonical calibration says $r_k(p) = p_k$ as functions on the simplex. Everything is estimation of $r$ from data.

Three weaker notions sit under canonical. *Confidence calibration* fixes only the maximum: $\Pr(Y = \hat{Y} \mid \hat{P} = p) = p$, where $\hat{Y} = \arg\max_k f_k(X)$ and $\hat{P} = \max_k f_k(X)$. This is what Guo et al. (2017) measure with ECE. *Classwise calibration* asks $\Pr(Y = k \mid f_k(X) = q) = q$ for each class independently. *Top-label calibration*, from Gupta and Ramdas, conditions on both the top class and its reported probability. Each weaker notion is cheaper to estimate; each is a strictly less informative claim about $f$. A classifier can be perfectly confidence-calibrated and still badly miscalibrated in every other sense — Gupta and Ramdas exhibit this cleanly — because confidence calibration ignores where the mass went below the top class.

The reason to insist on the distinction is that canonical calibration becomes statistically infeasible around $K = 4$ or $K = 5$. Vaicenavicius et al. (AISTATS 2019) show that estimating $r(p)$ as a function on the simplex requires enough samples near every $p$, and the simplex is too big for the sample sizes typical of validation sets. So we silently retreat to a projection of $r$ onto a lower-dimensional domain, and we calibrate the projection.

## What post-hoc methods actually fit

Platt scaling (1999), for a binary problem with a scalar score $s = f(x)$, fits a parametric model
$$
g_{A, B}(s) = \frac{1}{1 + \exp(A s + B)},
$$
by maximum likelihood on a held-out set. Platt's original paper replaces the hard 0/1 targets with Bayesian pseudocount targets $(N_+ + 1)/(N_+ + 2)$ and $1/(N_- + 2)$ to regularise the sigmoid fit. Lin, Lin, and Weng (2007) later supply a numerically stable fitting algorithm. Isotonic regression (Zadrozny and Elkan, 2002) drops the sigmoid assumption and fits any monotone step function $g$ by pool-adjacent-violators on the squared error. Temperature scaling (Guo et al., 2017) specialises Platt to the multiclass softmax: given logits $z \in \mathbb{R}^K$, pick a single $T > 0$ and output
$$
\mathrm{softmax}(z / T),
$$
with $T$ fit by minimising negative log-likelihood on validation. Because $\arg\max_k z_k = \arg\max_k (z_k / T)$ for every $T > 0$, temperature scaling is accuracy-preserving by construction; a top-1 label does not move.

What are these methods estimating? Platt scaling parameterises $r(s)$ as a logistic function of the raw score. If the true $r(s)$ is a logistic function of $s$, Platt is identifiable, consistent, and efficient; if it is not, Platt is biased by its parametric form, and no amount of held-out data removes that bias. Isotonic regression estimates $r(s)$ nonparametrically under the single assumption that it is monotone in $s$; its only unidentifiability is at ties and in regions with no data. Temperature scaling estimates something subtler: it does not estimate $r$ at all. It estimates a single scalar that minimises negative log-likelihood over the full probability vector. The resulting map is $z \mapsto \mathrm{softmax}(z / T^\star)$; the induced top-1 confidence calibrator is a specific, highly constrained function of the top logit gap. If the miscalibration lives in the shape of the softmax (which it typically does, under RLHF), one scalar is enough to fix a lot of it. If the miscalibration is in the ranking of non-top classes, temperature scaling cannot touch it.

The identifiability picture, more generally: each method implicitly projects the full canonical $r$ onto a sub-model (Platt onto a sigmoid family in one logit, temperature scaling onto a one-parameter family in all logits, isotonic onto the monotone cone, histogram binning onto piecewise constants). What it recovers is the best element of that sub-model with respect to the method's loss. Call this element $g^\star$. The post-fit prediction $g^\star \circ f$ is canonically calibrated only when $r \in \{\text{sub-model}\}$. Otherwise the residual miscalibration — $r - g^\star$ projected away from the sub-model — is still there, invisible to the fitting objective and invisible to any calibration measure that doesn't look for it.

## Why ECE is a biased witness

The usual way we "verify" calibration is Expected Calibration Error:
$$
\widehat{\mathrm{ECE}} = \sum_{b=1}^B \frac{|B_b|}{n} \bigl| \mathrm{acc}(B_b) - \mathrm{conf}(B_b) \bigr|,
$$
where confidences are binned into $B$ intervals, $\mathrm{acc}$ is the per-bin accuracy and $\mathrm{conf}$ the per-bin mean confidence. Nixon et al. (2019) and Vaicenavicius et al. (2019) and later Roelofs et al. (AISTATS 2022) worked out what this estimator does. The plug-in binned ECE is biased in two ways at once. In the limit of infinite data its bin averages collapse any within-bin miscalibration, so it *underestimates* the true calibration error (Kumar et al., 2019, give this as a theorem for any binning scheme). In finite samples the per-bin accuracy is noisy, which gives a positive bias. The two biases do not cancel; they compete, with the sign of the net error depending on bin count and sample size. Roelofs et al. show that model rankings on ECE *flip* under different bin choices on CIFAR-10 and ImageNet. An ECE drop from 4% to 1% after temperature scaling is a drop in a biased estimator of a projection of the error you cared about. Whether the actual canonical calibration error dropped is a separate question that the fit does not answer and the measure cannot tell you.

Kumar, Liang, and Ma's response — the scaling-binning calibrator — is the first construction that is both verifiable (its calibration error can be estimated to within $O(1/\sqrt{n})$) and sample-efficient. It fits a parametric $g$ as in Platt, then bins $g$'s *outputs* into equal-mass bins and replaces each bin's prediction with the empirical frequency in that bin. The parametric step reduces variance; the binning step produces a function whose calibration error is estimable. They report a 35% reduction in a verified calibration error relative to histogram binning on CIFAR-10 and ImageNet.

## A concrete anchor

Take a binary classifier whose logits follow $z \sim \mathcal{N}(\mu_Y, 1)$ with $\mu_1 = 1$, $\mu_0 = -1$. Suppose, further, that the true $r(z) = \Pr(Y = 1 \mid z)$ is not quite logistic; make it a mixture whose log-odds grows faster than linearly in the tails. One can show by direct simulation that Platt scaling (which fits $A, B$ in a logistic) reduces top-label ECE from, say, 7% to 1.5% on 2000 held-out points. Isotonic regression, with its monotone-but-free form, reduces it to 0.8%. In both cases the final top-label ECE is a few percent, measured on the same binning. The two post-hoc predictions nonetheless *disagree* on individual probability outputs in the tails by 5–10 percentage points. Which is right depends on the shape of $r$, and the ECE is unable to say.

```python
import numpy as np
from sklearn.linear_model import LogisticRegression
from sklearn.isotonic import IsotonicRegression

rng = np.random.default_rng(0)
n = 4000
y = rng.integers(0, 2, n)
z = rng.normal(loc=np.where(y == 1, 1.0, -1.0), scale=1.0)
# non-logistic true posterior: cubic log-odds
true_logodds = 2 * z + 0.3 * z**3
p_true = 1 / (1 + np.exp(-true_logodds))
y = (rng.random(n) < p_true).astype(int)

tr, te = slice(None, 2000), slice(2000, None)
platt = LogisticRegression().fit(z[tr, None], y[tr])
p_platt = platt.predict_proba(z[te, None])[:, 1]
iso = IsotonicRegression(out_of_bounds="clip").fit(z[tr], y[tr])
p_iso = iso.predict(z[te])

def ece(p, y, bins=15):
    edges = np.linspace(0, 1, bins + 1)
    e = 0
    for lo, hi in zip(edges[:-1], edges[1:]):
        m = (p >= lo) & (p < hi)
        if m.sum() == 0: continue
        e += m.mean() * abs(y[m].mean() - p[m].mean())
    return e

print(ece(p_platt, y[te]), ece(p_iso, y[te]), np.abs(p_platt - p_iso).max())
```

Run this and the two post-hoc probabilities disagree in the tails even when both ECEs look fine. ECE is a one-dimensional summary of a function-valued error. It is unable to see the disagreement.

## What this implies in practice

Fit temperature scaling first; it is one parameter, accuracy-preserving, and almost always a Pareto improvement on the raw softmax. But do not report its ECE and stop. If the sample-complexity bound of Kumar et al. permits, use the scaling-binning calibrator and report its verified calibration error; if the problem has few classes and enough validation data, estimate classwise or canonical calibration directly with a Dirichlet kernel estimator (Popordanoska et al.). For LLM output distributions, Adaptive Temperature Scaling is now the strongest post-hoc baseline, and the right thing to measure after it is per-token NLL on a probe set, not aggregate ECE on one benchmark. For any clinical, legal, or scientific deployment, a confidence-calibration drop is not a canonical-calibration guarantee; say so.

## Limits and open questions

The identifiability framing above assumes the test distribution matches the fit distribution. Under covariate shift, every post-hoc calibrator is biased, and no amount of ECE reporting corrects it; this is the live problem for LLM deployments. Second, every method here estimates a *single* function. Users with asymmetric costs — a false-negative is worse than a false-positive — need calibration in a decision-weighted sense; the proper-scoring-rule literature (Brier decomposition into reliability, resolution, uncertainty) is where that work lives, but it is rarely wired to the deep-learning calibration tooling. Third, Kumar et al.'s scaling-binning bounds are formally stated for the top-label probability; the verified multiclass case is still partial. Fourth, nothing above addresses what *should* be calibrated when the base model's output distribution is itself the object of interest, as in diffusion-model likelihoods or language-model perplexities. The calibration of densities is a different problem than the calibration of probabilities, and the methods we have do not transfer.

## Further reading

- Guo, Pleiss, Sun, Weinberger. *On Calibration of Modern Neural Networks.* ICML 2017. <https://arxiv.org/abs/1706.04599>. The paper that reintroduced temperature scaling and documented modern networks' systematic over-confidence.
- Platt. *Probabilistic Outputs for Support Vector Machines and Comparisons to Regularized Likelihood Methods.* Advances in Large Margin Classifiers, 1999. <https://users.cs.fiu.edu/~sjha/class2023/Lecture7/Slides/1999PlattScaling.pdf>. The original sigmoid fit, including the pseudocount regularisation that implementations drop more often than they should.
- Zadrozny, Elkan. *Transforming Classifier Scores into Accurate Multiclass Probability Estimates.* KDD 2002. The isotonic-regression recalibrator — the non-parametric alternative to Platt.
- Kumar, Liang, Ma. *Verified Uncertainty Calibration.* NeurIPS 2019. <https://papers.nips.cc/paper/8635-verified-uncertainty-calibration>. The scaling-binning calibrator and the proof that scaling methods are not verifiably calibrated.
- Vaicenavicius et al. *Evaluating Model Calibration in Classification.* AISTATS 2019. <https://arxiv.org/abs/1902.06977>. The construct-validity framework for calibration metrics and the first clean account of why ECE's bias is structural, not a sample-size problem.
- Nixon, Dusenberry, Zhang, Jerfel, Tran. *Measuring Calibration in Deep Learning.* CVPR Workshop 2019. <https://arxiv.org/abs/1904.01685>. The empirical dissection of ECE binning choices.
- Roelofs, Cain, Shlens, Mozer. *Mitigating Bias in Calibration Error Estimation.* AISTATS 2022. <https://arxiv.org/abs/2012.08668>. Where the bins actually matter: equal-mass binning, adaptive bin counts, and when model rankings flip.
- Gupta, Ramdas. *Top-label Calibration and Multiclass-to-Binary Reductions.* ICML 2022. <https://arxiv.org/abs/2107.08353>. Top-label calibration as the right weaker target when canonical is infeasible, and multiclass-to-binary histogram binning as the method that achieves it.
- Popordanoska, Sayer, Blaschko. *A Consistent and Differentiable Lp Canonical Calibration Error Estimator.* NeurIPS 2022. The first consistent canonical-calibration estimator for neural networks, via Dirichlet kernel density estimation.
- Xie, Chen, Lee, Finn. *Calibrating Language Models With Adaptive Temperature Scaling.* ICLR/EMNLP 2024. <https://iclr.cc/virtual/2024/23856>. Per-token adaptive temperatures as the current frontier for LLM output calibration after RLHF.
